newsitem.title: USA: WORLD BONDS - Aussie bonds beckon U.S. investors.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Aussie bonds beckon U.S. investors.

text.p: Australian bonds currently represent good value but could become an even better buy if U.S. Treasuries weather an anticipated interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve next week, U.S. experts said.
Australian bonds are "fairly valued" relative to U.S. Treasuries, said Richard Koss, international strategist at MFR Inc, an economic consulting and money management firm.
Any further rise in Australian bond yields to 8.25 and 8.30 percent would be a buy signal, especially if the Fed tightens and the U.S. Treasury curve flattens, Koss said.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan appeared to hint on Thursday the central bank was inching towards tightening credit. Fed policymakers are scheduled to meet on March 25.
Koss said the short-end of the Treasury curve could move higher, while the long-end might stabilize or even decline slightly if the market felt the Fed had acted preemptively to curb inflation.
Indeed the slope of the U.S. Treasury curve had narrowed to roughly 67 basis points on Friday morning from 71 basis points at Thursday's close and 77 basis points on Wednesday.

On Friday, the 10-year Australian bond was trading slightly above an 8.0 percent yield for a spread of about 127 basis points to comparable Treasuries. Spreads have already widened from around 80 basis points earlier in the year.

In prepared testimony to Congress' Joint Economic Committee on Thursday, Greenspan had said the U.S. economy retains a "great deal of vigor" and stressed the importance of preemptive action to ward off inflationary pressures.
Some U.S. investors pondered whether bonds might initially weaken next week if the Fed hikes rates. Bond prices tumbled when the Fed began a tightening cycle in February, 1994.

There may be some people that think there could be a replay of 1994 where yields backed up dramatically, said Michael Faust, a global portfolio manager at Bailard Biehl and Kaiser, which manages $350 million in fixed income securities.
"I don't see that happening at all, but I do think there certainly is a potential for a period of higher volatility and dislocation in the market," Faust said.
"Once you get in a period of some sort of stability with the bond market, then I think Australia will be very attractive," he added.
U.S. investors also cited tame inflationary pressures as one reason why Aussie paper is currently appealing.
Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Ian Macfarlane said on Thursday he saw the underlying inflation rate around the current level of 2.1 percent in the forseeable future.

"I think Australian bonds actually are a good value here," said Adam Greshin, a global bond portfolio manager at Scudder Stevens and Clark, which has more than $100 billion under management. "I don't have any particular target on where they need to go to."
Greshin said there is less need in Australia for higher interest rates because economic growth is not as strained as in the U.S. Their macro economic environment is quite healthy, he added.
